entry.title: Musk is not worth pandering to
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Musk is not worth pandering toMusk is not worth pandering to

India has good reason to keep satellite communications under the control of operators subject to Indian laws and security oversight

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

R Jagannathan6 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 11:14 PM ISTExamples of the pot calling the kettle black do not get more egregious than this. On Thursday, October 8, SpaceX’s trillionaire boss, Elon Musk, who can surely be called the super-oligarch among tech oligarchs, claimed that his Starlink satellite phone services were being blocked by India’s oligarchs.  He said on his social media platform X: “Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people… you can guess who they are…. This is a crime against the people of India”. An X account linked to Mr Musk went on to talk about how over 11,256 villages are without even 4G services as of May 2026. Rahul Gandhi, currently engaged in climbing barricades and protesting “vote chori”, unwisely appeared to endorse Mr Musk’s claim, with a “Welcome to India” post. The last thing one needs is an Indian politician batting for a foreign oligarch over far less powerful Indian ones.   Mr Musk is wide off the mark, not because India does not have oligarchs, but because the primary resistance to Starlink is not being driven by Mukesh Ambani of Jio or Sunil Mittal of Bharti Airtel, India’s telecom biggies, but the Government of India itself. The government is seriously concerned about the security ramifications of handing out satphones by the thousand to entities that could prove to be inimical to India.   Mr Musk may recall that when Starlink announced its intention to offer services in India, the first partners to tie up with him were the very same oligarchs he now rails against. The Modi government, to prevent a duopoly, has paid out or written off hundreds of crores in order to keep both Bharat Sanchar Nigam and Vodafone alive. If Mr Musk were really keen to serve the last man in India’s far-flung areas, he could easily have bailed out Vodafone himself and entrenched himself in the Indian telecom woodwork. But he didn’t. He wants to enter the Indian market both to make money and build political heft. With X, Grok (his artificial intelligence arm) and Starlink, he would be in a very powerful position to influence Indian politics.  The reality is that the overall market for satellite communications is likely to be very small initially. The official reason for allowing foreign satcom players to offer services in India is that regular telecom services in India’s interior and hilly regions are either poor or non-existent. But if one assumes that the people in these regions are also relatively poor, the paying market for such services is likely to be weak too — at least in the initial years.  The real market for satellite communication services (which include direct-to-phone internet services via satellite) will come in the following order: The state (armed forces, central and state police, administrators), followed by  politicians, businessmen, the urban rich and middle classes. The last four, mostly urban dwellers, do not need satphones when broadband Wi-Fi and 5G are already available to them.  For this category of potential users, a satphone would substantially be a vanity purchase like iPhones or folding mobile phones. But we cannot fail to add the one category that would want satphones as of yesterday: Smugglers and anti-social elements. So the pretence that satellite phones will be used to serve poor Arunachal goatherds is laughable. The rich always make their case by riding on the logic of helping the poor. Mr Musk is not going to give the Ladakhi citizen a satphone at  ₹199 a month rental.   The second reason why the oligarch argument does not quite hold is that the upfront investment in the business is huge. Both Sunil Mittal and Mukesh Ambani would have liked to ride on Mr Musk’s coattails rather than make those investments themselves. On the other hand, it was the government that nudged Mr Ambani to put up 1,600 near-Earth satellites in order to offer a home-grown alternative before Mr Musk wades in with his big bucks. The delays are probably deliberate on the government’s part, because it does not want Starlink to become so powerful in India before the domestic alternatives are made available. It is not the oligarchs who may be stalling Starlink, but the sovereign, which worries about internal and external security.  While Starlink has announced that it will comply with India’s security concerns, Mr Musk is a loose cannon with huge political opinions and interests. His Starlink has played a crucial role in the Ukraine-Russia war on the side of the former, and has even been known to pull services to Russians close to the warfront. He backs many Conservative and Right-wing governments in Europe and Latin America, including the now surging Alternative for Germany.   He was vociferous in demanding Keir Starmer’s resignation, and calling for a general election in the United Kingdom in January 2025. Mr Musk played a crucial role in consolidating the forces supporting Donald Trump in the 2024 Presidential elections, and it was only after he fell out with Mr Trump that his power in Washington ebbed. But in terms of money clout, he is George Soros raised to the power of 10: A businessman with the money and the intent to meddle in the politics of other countries.  Given the United States’ new-found willingness to slow down India’s economic rise and impede its ability to export more goods and services to America, there is no saying when Mr Musk will be used to needle and deter India. In fact, Mr Musk’s statement on oligarchs may make any Indian concessions to him on Starlink improbable. India has good reason to keep him away as long as possible.  India’s security concerns are real. Only anarchists will argue otherwise. There is a lot of political churn happening in India, and several sections of society are on the streets for various reasons (opposition parties, farmers, students, quota activists). The police forces in various states often use internet shutdowns to prevent rioting mobs from communicating with one another and making policing impossible. The easy availability of satphones with internet connections would make this method of crowd control impossible.   Also, the borders in the north and east are unstable, with large tribal and other populations freely moving across the Myanmar border. The availability of satphones in the hands of insurgents is a threat India cannot take lightly, and if we add the possibility of a politically-minded Starlink boss capable of using his power to impact politics in various countries, the delay in granting security clearance to Starlink is not difficult to understand.  There is a good case for satellite phones being totally in the hands of Indian businessmen who are subject to Indian laws and amenable to sovereign pressure to avoid aiding a breakdown in law and order or helping anti-social elements and insurgents. Keeping Elon Musk out would be an act of sovereign power, not oligarchic pressure. In this writer’s opinion, Mr Musk should never get a satellite licence in India.

entry.title: The making of brand Shashi Tharoor
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The making of brand Shashi TharoorThe making of brand Shashi Tharoor

The story of the man who makes you open a dictionary before breakfast is a masterclass in accidental differentiation

premium

Mr Tharoor’s brand lesson is simple: In a cluttered market, don’t try to be louder in the same language. Try to be different in a language only you can own (Photo:PTI)

Sandeep Goyal5 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 11:40 PM ISTIn India, there are two types of politicians. Type A: Those who rabble-rouse and make you clap or cry. Type B: Those who make you scratch your head and think. In a fun kind of way.   Shashi Tharoor single-handedly created Type B. And then made Type B more famous than Type A.  Ten years ago, he was a second-rung Congress MP from Thiruvananthapuram, known in Lutyens’ circles as “that UN guy who almost became Secretary General”. Respected, erudite, but not exactly someone your driver would discuss. Today, your driver knows him. Your cook knows him. Your 16-year-old knows him because he had to Google “sesquipedalian” after Mr Tharoor posted it on social media.  How did a diplomat with Oxford English become a mass brand in a country that loves three-word slogans? That’s Brand Tharoor. And it’s a masterclass in accidental differentiation. Mr Tharoor’s brand started in failure.  In 2006, he was India’s candidate for United Nations Secretary General. Shashi Tharoor vs Ban Ki-moon. He lost. Mr Tharoor should have won — suave, brilliant, author of five books, perfect UN English. But he didn’t. Most others would have retired to write columns.   Mr Tharoor did the opposite. He came back to India and joined politics — the one profession in India where good English is usually a disqualification.  In 2009, the Congress gave him Thiruvananthapuram. He won. Became minister of state for external affairs. Then came the first tweet that almost ended him. “Will travel in cattle class in solidarity with holy cows.” Talking about economy class. India erupted. In 2009, Twitter (now X) had 200,000 users in India. All of them were outraged. The headlines screamed: “Tharoor insults economy class passengers, calls them cattle.” He apologised.   But the brand was born — the English-speaking, slightly elitist, very witty man. Brand Tharoor pivoted from politician to phenomenon.  The real launch of Brand Tharoor was not a speech. It was a word. In July 2017, he tweeted: “Exasperating farrago of distortions, misrepresentations and outright lies.” India stopped. News anchors who had never used the word “farrago” in 20 years had to say it 20 times that evening. Memes exploded. School kids asked teachers — “What is farrago?”  And then Mr Tharoor did the smartest thing a brand can do — he owned it. He didn’t say: “Sorry for big words.” He launched “Tharoor’s Word of the Day.”  Farrago. Rodomontade. Sesquipedalian. Floccinaucinihilipilification — 29 letters, meaning the “act of estimating something as worthless”. He used it to describe something as worthless, using a word worthless to estimate worthlessness. Suddenly, every Indian who wanted to sound smart had a new guru. English teachers loved him. Tinder bios started saying: “Looking for someone who understands Tharoor without dictionary.”  This is classic brand differentiation. In a market where every politician was trying to be more desi, more simple, Mr Tharoor went the opposite way —  more complex, more English, more Oxford.  Byron Sharp would call it Distinctive Asset. In a sea of white kurta, Hindi slogan sameness, one man in a well-cut suit saying “snollygoster” stands out. You may not like him, but you cannot ignore him.  His English didn’t make him elite. It made him meme-able. In India today, meme-able is electable — at least for mindshare. From 2017 to 2020, Mr Tharoor became India’s most followed politician after Narendra Modi and Rahul Gandhi, without being Prime Minister, without being chief minister, without a single Hindi slogan. That’s not politics. That’s branding.  He turned vocabulary into virality.  The big words have both built and boxed him. For his fans, the words are proof of erudition. For his critics, the words are proof of elitism.  Mr Tharoor’s brand lesson is simple: In a cluttered market, don’t try to be louder in the same language. Try to be different in a language only you can own.  He didn’t try to out-Modi Modi in Hindi oratory. He didn’t try to out-Rahul Rahul in yatra. He owned English, books, wit — assets no one else could copy.  Second lesson: One distinctive word can be bigger than 100 speeches. Farrago did more for Mr Tharoor than 10 years of parliamentary questions.  Third lesson: Every strength, if overused, becomes your caricature. Mr Tharoor’s English got him famous, but now he has to work twice as hard to remind people he is more than English.  Brand Tharoor is not perfect. But it is lovable. In a country of 1.4 billion where most politicians sound the same, a man who makes you open a dictionary before breakfast has already won.  After all, as Mr Tharoor himself would say — his career is not an exasperating farrago, but a compelling case of rodomontade turned into relevance.  And you just Googled rodomontade, didn’t you?  That's Brand Tharoor.

entry.title: When the crops wilt
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / When the crops wiltWhen the crops wilt

The drought is almost providential for the ruling party as it postpones the hour of reckoning

premium

Seventy-five per cent of the state is officially stricken by drought and 82 per cent of agriculture is rain-fed with just 18 per cent irrigated area

Aditi Phadnis5 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 11:22 PM ISTIf it doesn’t rain in a few weeks, the rabi (winter-spring) agricultural season will also fail, and Maharashtra could be on the edge of a catastrophe after more than an 18 per cent deficiency in rain during the kharif (monsoon) season. Seventy-five per cent of the state is officially stricken by drought and 82 per cent of agriculture is rain-fed with just 18 per cent irrigated area.  Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis said last month: “We are bracing for severe drought, which could be worse than in 1972.” Revenue Minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule warned workers in Nagpur last month that “as the drought progresses, a bigger crisis will come upon Maharashtra. In fact, it will be bigger than the pandemic. There will be a shortage of water and fodder. You will see kharif and rabi wrecked. All crops will take a hit”. National Congress Party (SP) chief Sharad Pawar repeated the apprehension: “This year’s drought could be worse than in 1972.”  What happens to politics in a drought? Typically, it works out best for the ruling party. Take Mr Pawar. In terms of career progression, 1972 was not at all bad for him. He became a member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) for the first time from Baramati, and at 32, a state minister in charge of home and general administration in the Vasantrao Naik government. He was sent to other states to secure foodgrain for Maharashtra (he got a cold reception, he writes in his autobiography, from Uttar Pradesh because he refused to touch then chief minister Kamalapati Tripathi’s feet) but many other governments helped Maharashtra out. This eventually led to his star rising.  That 1972 drought was key to teaching India how to manage drought and food shortages. Maharashtra launched the Employment Guarantees Scheme (EGS) in 1969, the first state in India to do so. Research by economist Jean Dreze suggests that the poorest of the poor — agricultural landless labour — who were always the worst-hit in famines, found themselves relatively secure as a result of state intervention. The EGS provided this group a steady source of income and when, combined with the state’s robust public distribution system in the state, Maharashtra prevented the devastation that states like Bihar faced. True, the quality of the work and low payment, the quality of consumption, and the sudden injection of cash-fuelled consumption in a struggling rural economy had its own impact. But as economist Elizabeth Oughton observed in her research, some landless agricultural labour families “enjoyed” the drought because of the guarantee of work it represented.  More policy reform followed. Though only a junior minister, Mr Pawar scrapped the ban on the inter-district movement of fodder. Much later, came the construction of check dams (tiny dams built on nallahs) in the Prithviraj Chavan government (2009), cattle camps run by non-government organisations, and eventually the Drought Management Code (DMC) of 2026.  Although the DMC is rigorous in defining drought, its rollout apparently is not so much. Mahabaleshwar is one of the wettest towns in India. Yet it is on the list of talukas hit by drought and, therefore, eligible for drought relief. How could that happen? Although Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde represents an Assembly constituency in Thane, he belongs to the Mahabaleshwar taluka. And if every farmer — for instance — gets drought relief of ₹1 lakh per hectare and other benefits, so will farmers in Mahabaleshwar! By contrast, Kagal (represented by Hasan Mushrif in Kolhapur district), Shirdi (represented by Radhakant Vikhe Patil in Ahmadnagar district) and Dindori (represented by Narhari Zirwal in Nashik), among others, do not figure on the list, although all three are battling a severe shortage of water and crop failure. All three individuals belong to parties that are in the ruling alliance and are furious that their regions will not be eligible for drought relief.  So power, patronage and money fuel politics in drought: And the ruling party controls all of those. Climate-change activists can scream El Nino till they’re blue in the face. But the fact is, no one in Maharashtra is talking about “differences” between Mr Fadnavis and Mr Shinde for the moment. Instead, there is a wild scramble to get your constituency put on the drought-relief list. Crisis forces unity. In 1972, a young Sharad Pawar saw thousands of women led by Mrinal Gore, Ahilya Rangnekar and others take out the Laatni (rolling pin) morchas (processions) on Bombay streets, protesting against skyrocketing prices, beating empty tins with kitchen ladles.  All that is passe now.  In some ways, the drought is providential because it postpones the hour of reckoning in Maharashtra politics. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has no objection in principle to Mr Shinde, a Maratha, becoming chief minister. In fact, it badly needs a Maratha. But it would like him to merge his party, the Shiv Sena, into the BJP. Sena MLAs are against that move. Having won the Assembly elections and the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation polls pretty much on his own, Mr Fadnavis knows he is secure. But his followers and supporters are nudging him towards higher ambitions. A good drought is all things to all people!   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: The world is not the map
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The world is not the mapThe world is not the map

A UN-backed push for more accurate world maps highlights how every map involves compromises-and how the way we depict the Earth can shape our view of the world

premium

Africa is about 14 times larger than Greenland, a difference obscured by the commonly used Mercator map projection(Image: Wikimedia Commons)

Atanu Biswas5 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTWhile the Earth might be round, the map hanging on my wall is most definitely not. This seemingly innocent observation now has a fresh lease of political life. The United Nations General Assembly endorsed on September 4 an African-led resolution endorsing world maps depicting continents’ sizes proportionally more accurately. It, however, doesn’t ban Mercator projections nor mandate any other form of maps. It merely promotes the greater use of equal area maps, such as Equal Earth maps, especially when it comes to size representation.  The map that we grew up looking at doesn’t only show us locations of countries on Earth but also shapes our view of the world itself. But, let’s take an orange, peel it off delicately, and attempt to flatten all the peel out onto a tabletop. It wrinkles, rips, overlaps, or stretches. This simple experiment illustrates the problem of map-making from its beginning. The Earth is a curve, whereas paper is flat. One can cut and reassemble the peel, but cannot flatten it out completely without some modification. This phenomenon can be described in a reversed way, too: Try to cover an orange by a flat sheet of paper without distortion. Failure to do it doesn’t depend on the paper, but on geometry.  Nearly 200 years ago, in 1827, the legendary German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss offered a mathematical explanation to this problem by his Theorema Egregium. The curvature of the sphere is positive, and that of the plane is zero. Their geometrical natures are clearly different. Hence, while we project Earth, we have to give up something. We can keep form, area, some distance, or directions on our map. But we cannot keep all of them. There’s no ideal world map — that’s not a defect of cartography, but the effect of mathematics.  The map most of us use was invented by Gerardus Mercator in 1569. This map was extremely successful because of its practical uses — it was used for navigation as it preserved angles. In terms of its goal, it was an amazing creation. But Mercator has its noticeable drawback — sizes of objects become more and more exaggerated towards the poles. Take Greenland, which seems nearly the same size as Africa. It isn’t. Africa is actually 14 times larger. However, oddly enough, a projection intended for seafarers became the default map of the world in textbooks and also in practice.  An equal-area projection alters this perspective. Though, it doesn’t solve the problem from a mathematical standpoint. It just makes another kind of compromise. The Gall-Peters map preserves area but changes shape. Winkel Tripel tries to reduce multiple distortions. Though Goode Homolosine map projection maintains the proportion of sizes, the oceans have been split into pieces on the map. Equal Earth Projection was created by Tom Patterson, Bojan Savrič, and Bernhard Jenny in 2018. It retains relative size and maintains continent shape.  Which map, therefore, is the right one? Well, correct for what? A sailor would use one map, while a geographer would require another. A geography textbook will have yet another preference. Each map is an expression of the decision made on what to preserve and what to sacrifice.  However, each map is made with certain decisions in mind. Why is north at the top? Why is Europe in the middle? Why is the Pacific always shown on the margins? Nature doesn’t demand that “north” always be placed “up.” An upside-down map makes Australia appear at the top. Centre the Pacific, and the division between East and West starts looking like something completely different. The Earth remains the same. All that has changed is the frame around the picture. A map might begin geometrically, but it can become political.  Certainly one of the finest instances where humanity plays with the world is demonstrated in the movie The Great Dictator (1940) in which Charlie Chaplin played the Hitler-like character Adenoid Hynkel. In the film, Hynkel takes a globe, blows it up, and starts playing with it, throwing it up in the air. For a moment, the whole world is his toy. Then it bursts. While the sequence is comedic, there’s something strangely fitting about imagining the scene in relation to mapping. A globe keeps the curvature of the Earth; a map takes it away. Once the world is flattened, however, it becomes easier to reshape — shift boundaries, change centres, adjust scales. Maps have their own kind of power.  We shouldn’t, however, throw Mercator’s map in the dustbin of history. It still has its uses — for navigation and otherwise — wherever its attributes come in handy. Neither do we want to think that Equal Earth provides the solution. No map does so. Perhaps the truly honest answer is to appreciate the compromises in any map. This, perhaps, is the real message of the UN’s map debate. The earth will continue on just where it was before — round, huge, and completely unconcerned with the squabbles of the map-makers.

entry.title: Tata rift echoes beyond Bombay House
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Tata rift echoes beyond Bombay HouseTata rift echoes beyond Bombay House

A bigger stake once secured control, but businesses now see the need for a new playbook

premium

Bombay House

Amit Tandon5 min read Last Updated : Oct 08 2026 | 10:26 PM ISTIn 1983, Swraj Paul tried to take control of Escorts and Delhi Cloth and General Mills (DCM) by buying their shares on the market. By various accounts, he acquired 7.5 per cent in Escorts, while the Nanda family controlled around 5 per cent, and 13 per cent of DCM, compared with the Shri Ram family’s 10 per cent. Though Paul eventually withdrew his bid, the episode exposed how  many families controlled large companies with single-digit stakes until then, relying on the support of state-owned financial institutions. Their obvious response to this attack was to raise their ownership. Today, promoter shareholding in the Nifty500 averages around 50 per cent.  More than four decades later, the challenge for controlling-shareholders comes not from outside, but from within. On September 17, the Tata Sons board reappointed N Chandrasekaran and cleared the path to listing the company, over the opposition of Noel Tata, chairman of Tata Trusts, which owns 66 per cent of Tata Sons and seen as the keeper of its values, fears that a listing will dilute its charter.   Business families will read the dispute as a warning that ownership alone does not guarantee control of the boardroom, overturning an article of faith since 1983 — that a bigger stake is the surest defence. The fallout is likely to play out across at least four fronts.  First, more families may choose to keep control as chairperson  or in an executive capacity, rather than hand it to professional managers. A 2024 Deloitte study of 41 Nifty 50 companies (excluding public-sector enterprises) found that 31 were run by non-promoter chief executive officers and only 10 by promoters. Across India Inc as a whole, the share is likely to be lower still, given that about two-thirds of the S&P BSE 500 companies are family-owned. This episode could slow, or even reverse, the move towards professionalising businesses.  Will this impact India Inc’s performance? Families can point to evidence that ownership commitment pays. Credit Suisse’s Family 1000 research found that since 2006, family- or founder-owned listed companies have outperformed non-family companies by an annual average of 370 basis points. And in India, a study of 4,056 promoter-owned listed firms found that in group-affiliated companies, the level of promoter ownership had no effect on performance.  But the evidence cuts both ways. A landmark study of Danish firms found that when the CEO role passed to a family member, operating profitability fell by at least four percentage points. Even Credit Suisse found that family-owned companies score slightly lower on corporate governance than their non-family peers. A study covering 131 large listed Indian companies shows family firms with non-family CEOs performed better than those with family CEOs. Owning a company is different from running it.  Second, promoters may lean towards independent directors who are unlikely to challenge them. India’s problem is not too few independent directors but the wrong ones, appointed through processes that favour reputation over capability. Tuhin Kanta Pandey, chairman of the Securities and Exchange Board of India, has urged boards to recruit independent directors from beyond cosy networks and equip them to dissent, observing that “a board that never disagrees is not aligned — it’s asleep”. If promoters respond by packing boards with pliant directors, they will weaken the very oversight that minority shareholders rely on. And as one promoter told Business Standard, long-serving professionals can build fiefdoms and fill boards with people unlikely to challenge them.  Third, families will revisit their governance charters, since professionalising a board need not mean sidelining promoters. Companies will spell out who sets strategy, who executes it, and how disagreements are resolved, often through Articles of Association listing reserved matters that need promoter approval. Expect tighter affirmative voting rights, explicit rules on how nominee directors must vote, and clauses on replacing nominee directors and breaking board deadlocks, though nominees still owe their fiduciary duty to the company, not to whoever appointed them.  Yet drafting has limits. No document can fully anticipate a split within the owning family. And if affirmative rights written into charter documents do not hold, foreign direct investors, who rely on such rights, may grow more cautious.  Fourth, families will streamline their shareholding. Many groups still carry layers of crossholdings, investment companies and informal arrangements dating back decades. Families will collapse these into single holding vehicles, trusts or even individual names, to put control on a clearer legal footing. This is critical because today’s fault lines often run within families, not with outsiders — the Chhabrias at Finolex, the Kirloskars, the Kalyanis and Hiremaths — to name just a few.  These cases show how fragile even documented settlements, holding companies, trusts and wills can be.  In 1983, families protected control by raising their stakes. A bigger stake may not be enough if pressure comes from within. The current episode exposes friction that legal drafting cannot resolve. The businesses that come through will be those that plan succession early, apply their own rules consistently and leave management to professionals — they can work with. Such relationships rest on mutual trust and a shared long-term vision. The question now will no longer be whether someone is the best CEO in the market, but whether the controlling and minority shareholders, the boards and managements will align, to pull in the same direction.

entry.title: Geopolitical risks and monetary policy
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Geopolitical risks and monetary policyGeopolitical risks and monetary policy

Central banks need to factor in geopolitical risks before they materialise, not treat them as a sideshow

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

T T Ram Mohan6 min read Last Updated : Oct 08 2026 | 10:06 PM ISTLast May, the rupee came under pressure, rising above 96 to the dollar. In June, the Reserve Bank of India announced several measures to facilitate concessional swaps for foreign inflows, notably through the foreign currency non-resident (Bank) or FCNR(B) deposits. The expectation then was that these measures would result in inflows of around $50 billion and help ease the pressure on the rupee.  Your columnist had argued at the time that, given the outlook for oil prices and foreign institutional investor (FII) outflows, the inflow of funds under the RBI schemes would not suffice. A rise in the policy rate was inevitable. The inevitable has happened. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) opted for a 25 basis points increase in the repo rate on October 7.  The inflows under the RBI’s special measures amounted to a staggering $143 billion. Yet the rupee trades now at around 96.79 to the dollar. After a two-month hiatus, the exodus of FII funds resumed in September with net outflows of $6 billion.  The economic environment has changed materially in two respects since June. The price of crude oil has gone up from $85-90 to over $100 now. This is the price of oil futures. The market price of crude futures does not reflect the landed cost to India. The government’s chief economic advisor says that the price of India’s oil import basket is $114 today. That is an increase of 61 per cent over the average price of $71 in FY26. We now face oil prices well above our comfort range.  The second factor is the decision of the United States Federal Reserve last month to raise the policy rate by 25 basis points. The betting is that more rate hikes by the Fed are in the offing as inflation in the US remains above the target.   Any rise in Treasury yields affects India in two ways. One, it results in an exit of funds from emerging markets in general, which causes the rupee to depreciate. Two, it results in a narrowing of the yields on 10-year bonds in the US and in India. At 195 basis points, the difference in yields on 10-year government bonds is at its lowest in five years. This factor, too, contributes to the downward pressure on the rupee.  The RBI does not wish to defend any particular value of the rupee. Nevertheless, it has to respond to a sharp depreciation in the rupee because that can stoke domestic inflation.  The measures announced in June have not been able to contain the rupee’s depreciation. They ended up creating surplus liquidity in the system, about half of which has since been mopped up by the RBI. Surplus liquidity in the system renders the transmission of rate hikes that much more difficult.  Thus, by deferring a rate hike in June and August, the RBI is now having to deal with several issues: Higher oil prices, surplus liquidity, higher US Treasury yields, a narrower differential between long-term yields in the US and India, and a continued exodus of FII funds. A pre-emptive hike in the policy rate would have made its job easier. It would conceivably have eased the requirement for intervention through dollar sales in the foreign exchange market.  Monetary policy is said to be forward-looking. However, there is a serious limitation to how “forward-looking” is understood today. Central banks (and international agencies) tend to take a view on the economic situation, outline a baseline forecast and say it is subject to “geopolitical risks”.  In a world in which geopolitical risks are pretty much the norm, such an approach will not do. Central banks cannot afford to react to geopolitical risks — wars, sanctions, trade conflicts — after these have materialised. They will need to factor geopolitical risks explicitly into monetary policy, not treat them as a sideshow. How long will conflicts stretch out? What would that mean for energy prices and supply chain disruptions? Central banks need to ask and answer questions such as these in conducting monetary policy.  In June and August, the questions that needed to be asked were: One, does the US-Iran conflict have a reasonable chance of resolution? And, two, if it does not, what does that bode for oil prices? The answers should have been clear enough. The Iranian and American positions on the core issues were (and still are) so far apart that there was little chance of an amicable resolution. And that meant the continued disruption of oil supplies and an inexorable climb in oil prices to well above the $85-90 range. The implications of oil prices rising above $100 and staying there should have been factored into monetary policy.  Central banks need to create a Strategic Affairs unit that includes people with expertise in international relations, defence studies, the energy sector and economics. The idea is not to replicate the work done in ministries and intelligence agencies. Central banks cannot be in the business of forecasting wars. Rather, the unit must liaise with the concerned agencies and obtain and process geopolitical intelligence relevant to maintaining economic stability.  Central banks know how to respond if there is a major disruption that causes oil prices to rise to $120. What they need is a distribution of probabilities about the disruption. The MPC would have before it, say, a baseline forecast of oil prices of $85-90 per barrel with a 30 per cent probability that oil prices would rise to $120 following a major disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. It would then be better placed to judge whether a rate hike and the associated sacrifice of growth are justified.  The distribution of probabilities is precisely what the Strategic Affairs unit would seek to determine. The unit would convert the assessments it receives into scenarios for oil prices, inflation and exchange rates with probabilities attached to each scenario.   The RBI’s biannual Monetary Policy Report provides fan charts for inflation and gross domestic product  growth, indicating a range of outcomes. These are statistical probabilities based on historical modelling. What is required is scenario-building for current geopolitical risks of the sort outlined above.  Creating a Strategic Affairs unit would signal to the world that the appreciation of geopolitical risks has moved centre-stage at the RBI.

entry.title: Much needed policy adjustment
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Much needed policy adjustmentMuch needed policy adjustment

With inflation risks rising, RBI signals a measured tightening cycle ahead

premium

FY27 average has been increased by 20 bps to 5.2 per cent, while third quarter (Q3) and Q4 inflation forecasts have been increased by 10 and 20 bps, respectively, to 6 per cent and 5.7 per cent | File Photo

Indranil Pan New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 08 2026 | 1:02 AM ISTThe Reserve Bank of India (RBI) finally bites the bullet and delivers a much-needed 25 basis points (bps) repo rate increase. As per the arguments posited, the rate hike became essential as price pressures are seen to be broadening, as is indicated by the diffusion indices, where the share of items recording inflation above 4 per cent has increased to around 37 per cent as per the August reading.  Importantly, as was indicated by the central bank Governor Sanjay Malhotra, it is not only the headline inflation that is now being looked at, but core inflation is also under consideration for decision-making. The widening of the inflation pressures is evident in the exclusion-based measures of core inflation too. CPI excluding food, fuel and precious metals has consistently moved up from the beginning of the current financial year (FY27), when it was at 2.2 per cent, to record 2.9 per cent in August.  The assessment on the inflation dynamics is that pressure will continue from the supply side — both on account of the deficient southwest monsoons that are also expected to have implications for rabi cropping due to lower soil moisture levels and weak reservoir levels in certain pockets. The expression of the inflation concerns comes out through the change in projection on inflation for the remaining part of the year.  FY27 average has been increased by 20 bps to 5.2 per cent, while third quarter (Q3) and Q4 inflation forecasts have been increased by 10 and 20 bps, respectively, to 6 per cent and 5.7 per cent. On the other hand, the assessment on growth for FY27 has been increased to 7.1 per cent from 6.7 per cent earlier, thereby providing the platform for the RBI to push the pedal on rates without worrying too much on the growth sacrifice. More important than the policy action, which was already in the price, was the forward guidance on rates. Crucially, with a 4:2 majority, the stance was changed from “neutral” to “calibrated tightening”.  We must wait for the minutes to understand the minds of the dissenters. However, as explained by the Governor, a “calibrated tightening” would mean a milder form of tightening that will be more measured and after having taken into consideration the evolving conditions on the growth-inflation mix. Clearly, though, a cut is off the table — something that was a possibility when the stance was “neutral”.  After the rate hike has started, the immediate question on everyone’s minds — how many and at what frequency. Traditionally, economists, including myself, look for a real rate of around 1 per cent over the longer-term inflation forecast to arrive at the nominal terminal rate. By this method, RBI can be expected to hike by an additional 100 bps to bring the terminal rate to 6.5 per cent. Having said that, at the presser Gupta clarified that the real rate is a theoretical construct, difficult to estimate and thus cannot necessarily guide monetary policy.  Thus, going forward, the RBI will evaluate data developments both domestically and internationally to incrementally decide on the rate structure. For now, I would bet on two more rate hikes of 25 bps each in the current cycle.

entry.title: Airline safety grounded in terra firma
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Airline safety grounded in terra firmaAirline safety grounded in terra firma

Air passengers pay for their safety in the skies one way or another - even though the real solution lies in the hands of politicians

premium

The flydubai near-tragedy showed how the gratuitous conflicts their governments started in West Asia have made the world unsafe for them | Image: Bloomberg

Kanika Datta5 min read Last Updated : Oct 07 2026 | 10:49 PM ISTThe close call for 174 passengers travelling on flydubai flight FZ1073 has provoked a flood of suggestions from the global commentariat on enhancing airline security. But history suggests that no security measures can be 100 per cent disaster-proof as long as global politics remains in turmoil.  In fact, only a rare trifecta of good fortune ensured that there were no fatalities on board the flydubai flight from Dubai to Israel, which resulted from the depredations of a suicidal Omani pilot with anti-Israeli inclinations. The courageous Captain Smit  Machchhar, who, despite severe head injuries, managed to unlock the cockpit door and alert passengers to the crisis; a plumber who was familiar enough with aircraft controls to steady the plummeting aircraft because he closely followed Air Crash Investigation; and, finally, the presence of two off-duty pilots who took charge and made an emergency landing.  Many have drawn obvious parallels between the unforeseen exigency of a mentally disturbed pilot with murderous intentions against the mainly Israeli passengers on flight FZ1073 and the serial 9/11 hijackings by fundamentalists armed with box cutters. All of these crimes were designed as high-impact revenge against the country or countries that had launched an invasion against their own. A frisson of fear is now bound to travel through Israelis and their American allies about the wisdom of air travel. The flydubai near-tragedy showed how the gratuitous conflicts their governments started in West Asia have made the world unsafe for them (and unfortunate co-passengers of other nationalities). Those with longer memories will remember an earlier time in the 1970s when disaffected Palestinian guerrilla groups almost routinely hijacked airliners flying to or from Israel or the United States.  On September 6, 1970, for instance, Palestinian guerrillas hijacked four aircraft bound for New York in a coordinated action that shook the world — a TWA flight travelling from Frankfurt, El Al and Pan Am flights from Amsterdam, and a Swissair flight from Zurich. One of those hijackings failed thanks to the presence of mind of the pilot Uri Bar, though he is less remembered than the glamorous AK-47-wielding Leila Khaled, a member of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) and veteran of a 1969 hijacking. One of the aircraft was diverted to Beirut and two landed in Jordan, where they were surrounded by the Jordanian army. The PFLP was demanding the release of Palestinians held in Germany, Switzerland, England and Israel within 72 hours or they would kill all the hostages.  As the US flew in the 82nd Airborne and the Sixth Fleet was put on standby, the long standoff — which included the hijacking of a British Overseas Airways Corporation aircraft the next day — saw the outbreak of the famous “Black September” war between the Jordanian military and Yasser Arafat’s Palestinian Liberation Organisation. It ended after Egypt’s Nasser Hussein brokered a deal that saw the hostages released and the hijackers set free.  Afterwards, American journalist Walter Cronkite presciently commented that the Palestinian guerrillas “thrust back to the world’s attention a problem diplomats have tended to shove aside …”  Two years later, Palestinian guerrillas hijacked a Sabena Air flight to Tel Aviv. It was during the rescue operation that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin  Netanyahu, then a commando, gained fame for his heroics in foiling the plot. Four years later, he lost a brother in Operation Thunderbolt, when Israeli commandos famously stormed a hijacked Air France flight that was diverted to Entebbe, Uganda.  Back in India, little of this international drama registered on airport security. Air travel was rare in those days anyway, involving only a minuscule proportion of India’s population. Security checks mostly consisted of personnel perfunctorily checking hand luggage and occasionally asking if you were carrying knives or bombs. Children in those days freely visited the cockpit, where friendly pilots showed you the controls and gave you sweets. All that abruptly ended in 1985 when a bomb, planted by Punjab militants, exploded aboard the Emperor Kanishka, sending 329 people to the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean. Metal detectors now made their presence felt and tarmac identification of checked-in luggage became the norm.  The IC 814 hijacking of 1999 — another casualty of botched diplomacy and intelligence — made baggage screening compulsory. After the 9/11 tragedies, cockpit doors were securely locked from the inside. Tragically, that policy sent 150 people plunging to their deaths when a mentally unhinged co-pilot locked his captain out of the cockpit and crashed Germanwings Flight 9525 into the French Alps in 2015. Passengers on flydubai flight FZ1073 may have suffered a similar fate were it not for Captain Machchhar.  The upshot of growing insecurity in the skies has been skyrocketing expenditure on security by airport operators. By one reckoning, security alone accounts for 20 per cent of airport operators’ expenditure. Some airports pass this cost on to passengers either wholly or partly. In short, air passengers pay for their security in the skies one way or another — even though, as Cronkite pointed out 56 years ago, the real solution lies in the hands of leaders and politicians on terra firma.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Hawkish hike, but measured path ahead
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Hawkish hike, but measured path aheadHawkish hike, but measured path ahead

Depending on growth-inflation dynamics, the repo rate could rise to 6-6.25 per cent next year

premium

A December rate hike looks all but certain, after which the MPC is likely to proceed in a measured way | File Photo

Tamal Bandyopadhyay7 min read Last Updated : Oct 07 2026 | 10:45 PM ISTAs expected, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), the rate-setting body of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), has raised the policy repo rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 5.5 per cent. It has also changed its stance to “calibrated tightening”.  The six-member MPC voted unanimously for the hike, while the change in stance was carried by a 4-2 vote.  The RBI rarely describes its stance as “calibrated tightening”. The usual descriptors are “accommodative” and “neutral”; during the 2022-23 tightening cycle, it used “withdrawal of accommodation”.  The MPC first adopted a “calibrated tightening” stance in October 2018, under then-RBI governor Urjit Patel, moving from “neutral” while keeping the repo rate unchanged at 6.5 per cent amid rising international crude oil prices and foreign exchange volatility. The December 2018 policy retained the stance, again with no rate action.  In February 2019, as inflationary pressures abated, the stance was changed back to “neutral” and the policy rate was cut by a quarter of a percentage point to 6.25 per cent. By then, Shaktikanta Das was at the helm of the central bank.  Governor Sanjay Malhotra’s statement that “rate cuts are off the table in the near term and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause, depending on the evolving conditions and the outlook” has triggered an intense debate on the length of the current rate hike cycle. Most analysts are pencilling in a further three-quarters to one percentage point of hikes, which would take the policy rate to 6-6.25 per cent.  A December rate hike looks all but certain, after which the MPC is likely to proceed in a measured way. That is why the stance is “calibrated tightening”. The governor’s statement says: “The duration and extent of the rate hike cycle would be contingent on the actual growth-inflation developments and outlook, especially that of underlying inflation, the extent of broadening of price pressures and second round effects of the supply shock, as also the impact of demand impulses.”  The RBI last raised the repo rate in February 2023, to 6.5 per cent. After holding it there through 2023 and 2024, it cut the rate by a cumulative 125 basis points (bps) between February and December 2025. One basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point.  On Wednesday, the broader equity market slipped, but the Bank Nifty rose initially, as banks are expected to raise lending rates, which will boost their net interest margins. Nifty and Sensex closed 0.75 per cent and 0.58 per cent lower, respectively; Bank Nifty closed marginally lower. With the financial system flush with liquidity, deposit rate hikes will have to wait. Transmission of the rate hike cycle for depositors will not be overnight, while the loan cost will rise fast for the borrowers.  The 10-year government bond yield rose to a three-year high at 7.24 per cent and, despite the rate hike, the rupee slipped to 96.77 against the dollar.  The RBI has raised both its growth and inflation projections for the current financial year and given its estimates for the first quarter of the next year.  Citing continued supply-side pressures from a deficient southwest monsoon, El Niño conditions and high volatility in international oil prices, the RBI said: “inflation and its outlook are not benign”. It has projected consumer price index inflation for FY27 at 5.2 per cent and core inflation at 4.4 per cent. Inflation is expected to peak at 6 per cent in the third quarter, and the estimate for the first quarter of FY28 is 5.6 per cent.  These estimates give a sense of how far the current cycle could run. With inflation projected at 6 per cent in the third quarter and 5.6 per cent in the first quarter of next year, the policy rate needs to rise to 6-6.25 per cent to keep the real interest rate positive.  Incidentally, the monetary policy statement does not give an estimate of the crude oil price. In the June and August reviews, the RBI maintained a baseline assumption of $85 per barrel for its 2026-27 projections. But the Monetary Policy Report, released alongside the policy on Wednesday, has revised the assumption to $95 per barrel for the second half of the year.  The price of the Indian crude basket rose from $82 a barrel in July to around $114-116 a barrel in September.  The RBI has raised its real gross domestic product (GDP) growth projection for FY27 by 40 bps to 7.1 per cent. After a strong showing in the first two quarters, growth is expected to slow in the second half. Real GDP growth for the first quarter of FY28 is also projected at 7.1 per cent.  This is in line with the estimates of most global agencies. The World Bank and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development have both raised their India growth forecasts for the current financial year to 7.1 per cent. S&P Global Ratings, the Asian Development Bank and Moody’s project 7 per cent, while Fitch Ratings has pegged it at 6.9 per cent.  For both inflation and GDP growth, the “risks are evenly balanced”.  Following $143.6 billion of foreign exchange inflows through the special swap facility opened in June, the banking system has seen a daily average liquidity surplus of ₹5.9 trillion since the last MPC meeting in August, though this has moderated recently.  Malhotra did not outline a specific tool to absorb liquidity, but said: “The Reserve Bank will use an appropriate mix of liquidity management tools and strive to align the weighted average call rate with the policy repo rate.”  To absorb excess cash from the banking system, the RBI has been selling government bonds through open market operations and holding variable rate reverse repo auctions. Malhotra said it would continue to do so, and that raising banks’ cash reserve ratio (CRR), the portion of deposits banks must keep with the RBI without earning interest, would be the last resort. Fresh FCNR(B) deposits mobilised under the special scheme have been exempted from both CRR and the statutory liquidity ratio.  In his post-policy media interaction, Malhotra also referred to the central bank’s dollar sales to keep the rupee stable, which also helps drain liquidity from the system. Asked about the value of the rupee against the dollar, he said: “By a number of estimates, including the REER, the rupee is not overvalued; it may be undervalued.”  REER stands for real effective exchange rate. It’s the weighted average of a currency’s value against a basket of trading partners’ currencies, adjusted for inflation differences between them, and is a measure of trade competitiveness. The RBI’s six-currency REER basket covers roughly 40 per cent of India’s foreign trade, while the broader 40-currency index covers about 88 per cent of its merchandise trade.
